chunks.content: Introduction Patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), the final stage of chronic kidney disease, require kidney replacement therapies such as hemodialysis (HD), peritoneal dialysis (PD), or kidney transplantation to replace essential kidney functions [ ]. Among them, PD is a process that involves inserting a catheter into the peritoneal cavity to filter fluids and waste products [ ]. One of the main advantages of PD is that patients themselves can perform the procedure, thus making it preferred by some ESKD patients due to its convenience and enhanced mobility. However, the procedure is associated with a risk of infection, and the source of the infection is not only the vulnerable catheter structure but also the patients with kidney failure who have compromised immunity [ , ]. PD is a technique that needs the patient or a caregiver to be in a condition to carry out the process independently. Therefore, it may not be suitable for all ESKD patients [ ]. Proper catheter management, particularly maintaining sterility, is important. Contamination during the PD exchange procedure must be avoided since it can lead to PD-related infections such as peritonitis, exit-site infection (ESI), and tunnel infection (TI), which affect patient survival and long-term treatment success [ , ]. Over the past few years, pet ownership has been on the rise worldwide, and South Korea is no exception to the trend despite the country’s decreasing birth rates. For example, the dog population in South Korea increased by 44.6% between 2019 and 2022, and more than 3 million dogs were registered in the country within this period [ ]. The number of PD patients who own pets is also increasing, and about 30% of the PD households have pets in the global Peritoneal Dialysis Outcomes and Practice Patterns Study (PDOPPS) [ ]. Although there is limited research on whether or not pet ownership is associated with peritoneal dialysis-related infections, the most recent International Society for Peritoneal Dialysis (ISPD) peritonitis guidelines specifically warn of contamination from indoor pets[6]. There were cases of bacterial peritonitis events that were caused by zoonotic organisms from pets through animal bites or scratches [ – ]. Nevertheless, the question of whether pet ownership is associated with PD-related infections remains open since there is a study that found that the presence of pets does not lead to an increased risk of peritonitis, except for patients who have cats and dogs [ ]. More studies are needed to determine the potential of pets in the contribution to infections due to zoonotic organisms and the long-term impacts on PD patients. Therefore, our study aims to investigate the characteristics of PD-related infections according to pet ownership status, including incidence, causative organisms, and clinical outcomes. Materials and methods Study population This study was a retrospective single-center cohort study conducted at Soonchunhyang University Cheonan Hospital, involving patients on PD from January 2016 to December 2023. We included patients with a follow-up period exceeding 6 months, as well as those who transitioned to HD or deceased within 6 months ( ). The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Soonchunhyang University Cheonan Hospital (IRB No. 2023-07-049) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki of the World Medical Association. The IRB waived the need for informed consent from participants due to the retrospective nature of the study and the use of de-identified data. Clinical data collection The medical records of the study subjects were reviewed to collect demographic information such as age, gender, duration of dialysis, body mass index (BMI), pet ownership, PD modality, and the etiological cause of ESKD. Data were accessed for research purposes from 03/04/2024 to 10/12/2025. Age was based on the time of initial enrollment, and pet ownership was confirmed based on the observations of PD nurses during home visits. Additionally, laboratory test results recorded at the initial time point during the observation period, including hemoglobin, glucose, albumin, total cholesterol, triglycerides, potassium, phosphorus, total calcium, C-reactive protein, and 24-hour urine volume, were also gathered. Furthermore, events of peritonitis, ESI, and TI occurring during the observation period were documented, including details on the causative organisms, occurrence of catheter removal, and mortality. Detailed data underlying these events are provided in S10 and S11 Tables in in the Supporting Information. When multiple organisms were isolated from ESIs, the primary pathogen was specifically selected as multiple isolates are common in catheter-related infections near the skin [ ]. The criteria for identifying the primary pathogen of ESI were based on the organism that appeared most frequently and in the highest quantities in repeated tests conducted during the same period. In our center, patients undergoing PD were routinely educated regarding pet-related precautions. They were advised to keep pets separate from the dialysis environment as a general measure, and specifically to avoid close proximity to pets during dialysis

When multiple organisms were isolated from ESIs, the primary pathogen was specifically selected as multiple isolates are common in catheter-related infections near the skin [ ]. The criteria for identifying the primary pathogen of ESI were based on the organism that appeared most frequently and in the highest quantities in repeated tests conducted during the same period. In our center, patients undergoing PD were routinely educated regarding pet-related precautions. They were advised to keep pets separate from the dialysis environment as a general measure, and specifically to avoid close proximity to pets during dialysis exchanges. Exit-site care was performed in accordance with the recommendations of the ISPD, including routine exit-site cleansing and standard prophylactic measures [ ]. Outcomes The diagnostic criteria for peritonitis, ESI, and TI adhered to the most recent ISPD guidelines [ , ]. According to these guidelines, a definitive exit-site infection is characterized by the presence of purulent discharge. Therefore, catheter-related events without discharge, but with other inflammatory signs such as erythema, tenderness, or swelling, were not included as infection events. Additionally, relapsing peritonitis, ESI, and TI are excluded from the infection events, as they are considered extensions of the original episode. Relapsing infection events were defined as infections occurring within 4 weeks of completing therapy for a prior episode with the same organism or culture-negative episode. Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 25.0. Categorical variables such as gender, pet ownership, and the etiologic cause of ESKD were expressed as counts (percentages). Continuous variables such as duration of dialysis, BMI, and laboratory parameters were presented as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range), as appropriate. For comparisons between two groups, the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test was used for categorical variables, while the Mann-Whitney U test was employed for continuous variables. Incidence rate was defined as events per person-year, with 95% confidence interval (CI) calculated by the mid-P exact test. Missing data were excluded without imputation. Results Baseline characteristics Baseline characteristics of pet owners and non-pet owners are present in , with a breakdown by pet types detailed in S1 Table in . Among the 162 patients, 24 patients raised pets, including 8 cat owners and 16 dog owners. The specific number of pets and whether they were kept indoors or outdoors are presented in S2 Table in . No significant differences in clinical features were observed between pet owners and non-pet owners. The median follow-up duration was 3.00 years (0.94–4.98) for cat owners, 2.67 years (1.09–4.22) for dog owners, and 3.05 years (1.23–5.72) for patients without pets. Zoonotic peritonitis were observed in pet owners During the follow-up period, 2 cases of peritonitis caused by zoonotic organisms were noted ( , S3 and S4 Tables in ). These cases involved a cat owner infected with Pasteurella dagmatis , and a dog owner infected with Pantoea agglomerans . The case of Pantoea agglomerans infection is detailed further in a case report [ ]. Notably, both patients were undergoing automated peritoneal dialysis (APD). When examining the incidence rate of peritonitis, pet ownership (Incidence Rate = 0.20 events/person-year, 95% CI 0.12–0.31, ) did not result in a higher peritonitis rate compared to patients without pets (Incidence Rate = 0.28 events/person-year, 95% CI 0.24–0.33, ). Further analysis by pet type revealed similar findings: both cat owners (Incidence Rate = 0.26 events/person-year, 95% CI 0.13–0.46, S3 Table in ) and dog owners (Incidence Rate = 0.15 events/person-year, 95% CI 0.06–0.29, S3 Table in ) showed no significant differences in peritonitis rates compared to non-pet owners. The occurrence and causative organisms of peritonitis events for each patient are listed in S5 Table in . Additionally, regarding prognosis following peritonitis, no significant differences were observed between patients with or without pets (S6 and S7 Tables in ). Across the entire cohort, 6 peritonitis-related deaths and 16 catheter removal events were recorded during the observation period. Staphylococcus-associated exit-site infections according to pet ownership When analyzing ESI events, a distinct pattern was observed in the microbiological profile of infections based on pet ownership. Among pet owners, Staphylococcus species were the major pathogens responsible for 5 out of 9 ESI events, more frequently observed compared to non-pet owners (55.6 vs. 16.2%, p = 0.006, ). Furthermore, 4 out of 5 Staphylococcal ESI events in pet owners were in cat owners (S8 Table in ). Meanwhile, the presence of pets did not significantly affect the overall incidence rate of ESI events ( ). Further analysis of dog ownership and cat ownership revealed consistent results, showing no significant differences (S8 Table in ). The occurrence and causative organisms of ESI events for each patient are listed in S9 Table in . Tunnel infection associated with pet ownership During the follow-up period, a total of 6 TI events were observed, with 2 occurring in pet owners ( ). Notably, the patients with these infections were both cat owners. Expressed as proportions by group, 2.4% of non-pet owners (4 of 138), 8.3% of pet owners overall (2 of 24), and 25.0% of cat owners specifically (2 of 8) experienced TI. TI cases in cat owners presented with distinctive clinical features: the patient in case 1 experienced 3 additional ESI events along with the TI during the follow-up period, while the patient in case 2 had catheter reposition following the TI. Meanwhile, the other patients experienced either one additional ESI (cases 2–4) or none (cases 5 and 6). However, no catheter removal was required due to TI in pet owners, whereas TI led to catheter removal in three other patients. Discussion Our study investigated PD-related infection profiles by pet ownership status, such as peritonitis, ESI, and TI. The study results showed that zoonotic peritonitis was observed during the follow-up period. Moreover, Staphylococcus-associated ESIs were more frequently observed among patients with pet ownership in this cohort. Lastly, 33% of TIs during the follow-up period were descriptively noted in pet owners, with one requiring catheter reoperation. The most recent ISPD guideline recommends the need for additional precautions to prevent peritonitis in the presence of indoor pets [ ]. Specifically, they highlight the risk of infections caused by zoonotic organisms through close contact with companion animals. Our study also identified cases of peritonitis caused by zoonotic organisms, including Pasteurella dagmatis and Pantoea agglomerans . Pasteurella species is a microorganism commonly colonized in cats, which can be transmitted through bites or scratches [ ]. Because APD requires long external tubing and a warming plate that may attract pets, patients undergoing this modality may be more vulnerable to pet-related contamination. Consistently, within our cohort, both patients with zoonotic infections in our study were on APD. These observations suggest that awareness of potential pet-related injuries may be particularly relevant for patients with pet ownership undergoing APD [ ]. In addition, Staphylococcus-associated ESIs were more frequently observed among patients with pet ownership in this cohort. Globally, including Korea, Staphylococcus is reported as the most common causative organism for ESIs, responsible for 30–50% of cases [ – ]. Even though coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species generally pose a relatively lower risk and can be managed with appropriate antibiotics according to the clinical context, Staphylococcus aureus , particularly methicillin-resistant strains, exhibits high virulence and antibiotic resistance and requires careful management. Accordingly, the use of prophylactic agents and the implementation of preventive strategies have been recommended to reduce the risk of Staphylococcus-associated ESIs [ ]. Previously, based on data from the Korea PDOPPS study, we demonstrated that xerosis is significantly associated with an elevated risk of ESIs, with a particularly pronounced increase in the risk of S. aureus -associated ESIs [ ]. Notably, the relative abundance of S. aureus within the skin microbiota of dialysis patients was higher under xerotic conditions, potentially explaining the increased susceptibility to ESIs observed with greater xerosis severity [ ]. Moreover, our previous study identified pet ownership as a significant risk factor for xerosis in PD patients. Pet-related substances, including saliva and dander, have been suggested to compromise skin integrity or alter the skin microbiome of patients [ , ]. Against this background, pet ownership may be considered a contextual factor when interpreting the characteristics of Staphylococcus-associated ESIs in PD patients, based on descriptive observations from the present study. Lastly, a proportion of TI events (33%) was descriptively observed among patients with pet ownership, particularly cat owners. Due to the limited number of events, no conclusions can be drawn regarding the relationship between pet ownership and TI. Even so, we confirmed that pet ownership, whether of a cat or a dog, did not increase the incidence of peritonitis or ESI events among patients at this center. This finding aligns with previous findings, including recent global PDOPPS studies, that also explored the relationship between pet ownership and peritonitis [ , ]. Additionally, our findings indicate that the prognosis of peritonitis is unaffected by pet ownership. This finding aligns with previous findings, including recent global PDOPPS studies, that also explored the relationship between pet ownership and peritonitis [ , ]. Additionally, our findings indicate that the prognosis of peritonitis is unaffected by pet ownership. Pet ownership offers numerous emotional benefits, potentially enhancing long-term outcomes by improving well-being and life satisfaction [ ]. Emotional stability is especially crucial for dialysis patients as it can significantly enhance their quality of life and prognosis, and we have investigated this issue extensively in our studies [ , ]. Consequently, instead of restricting pet ownership, attention to hygiene and avoidance of potential injuries may be important for patients who keep pets [ ]. This study has several limitations. First, despite using data from patients treated at this center over an extended period of eight years, the small number of pet owners (n = 24) and the relatively low incidence of PD-related infections limited the statistical power to detect meaningful differences, increasing the risk of a type II error. Therefore, the absence of a significant association between pet ownership and infection risk should be interpreted with caution. In addition, multivariable adjustment for potential confounders—such as diabetes, dialysis vintage, PD modality, nutritional status, and residual kidney function—was not performed due to the limited sample size and number of events, and residual confounding cannot be excluded. To provide more robust clinical evidence, an analysis involving a larger population is necessary. Moreover, pet ownership was determined based on observations made by PD nurses during home visits. In cases where pets were not visible during these visits, there is a possibility that some instances of pet ownership may have been missed. In addition, detailed information regarding pet exposures—such as the level of contact with PD equipment, access to the dialysis room, and history of pet-related injuries—was not systematically collected. As a result, the degree of exposure to potential zoonotic pathogens could not be fully assessed. Therefore, all subgroup and pathogen-specific findings should be interpreted as exploratory. Nevertheless, to our knowledge, our study is the first to describe PD-related infection characteristics in the context of pet ownership in Korea. With the global increase in pet ownership, including in Korea, understanding the impact of pets on PD patients is becoming more crucial than ever. Further research is needed to better assess the influence of pets on PD outcomes. Supporting information S1 File Supplementary materials including Tables S1–S11. (DOCX)

Introduction The global adoption of peritoneal dialysis (PD) has increased significantly in recent decades, with particularly rapid expansion in China, Thailand, and the United States [ ]. This growth has heightened the importance of optimizing PD quality to ensure sustainable patient outcomes. Peritonitis persists as the leading cause of PD technique failure worldwide [ ], underscoring the critical need to identify modifiable risk factors for peritonitis prevention. Patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) and end-stage kidney disease (ESRD) commonly exhibit dyslipidemia [ , ]. Recent advances in lipid biology have revealed novel roles for lipoproteins in immune regulation and infection defense [ – ]. Of particular interest, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) has demonstrated potentially protective functions in inflammatory and infectious processes through multiple mechanisms [ , ]. Despite these biological insights, the relationship between HDL-C concentrations and the risk of peritoneal dialysis-related peritonitis (PDRP) remains insufficiently investigated. To date, only a limited number of studies have explored this association in PD patients. Szeto et al. [ ] observed that the combination of low HDL-C ( < 1 mmol/L) and diabetes mellitus increased PDRP risk; however, their multivariate regression model did not directly evaluate the association between HDL-C concentrations and peritonitis risk. Similarly, Wang et al. [ ] reported no significant association between HDL-C concentrations and peritonitis risk, but their analysis was limited to assessing HDL-C as a continuous variable for linear association, without examining potential differences in PDRP risk across clinically relevant HDL-C strata. Notably, these studies [ , ] did not account for several important confounding variables, including C-reactive protein (CRP) concentrations, total weekly Kt/V, and total weekly creatinine clearance (CrCl), which may substantially influence the results. Consequently, the relationship between HDL-C concentrations and PDRP risk in PD patients remains unclear. To address these knowledge gaps and elucidate the potential clinical significance of HDL-C, we conducted a comprehensive investigation examining the association between HDL-C concentrations and new-onset PDRP risk in maintenance PD patients. Methods Study design and population This retrospective single-center cohort study included 672 patients who initiated PD at the Peritoneal Dialysis Center of Nanfang Hospital, China, between January 1, 2010 and December 31, 2020. The study protocol was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of Nanfang Hospital (NFEC-2010–78). Informed consent was waived for this retrospective study by the institutional review board. We excluded patients with: (1) PD duration < 3 months; (2) missing baseline data on dialysis regimens or lipid profiles; (3) history of kidney transplantation; (4) > 1 year of hemodialysis history; or (5) peritonitis within 30 days post-PD catheter insertion. After these exclusions, 512 patients were included in the final analysis (Fig. ). Included and excluded subjects had comparable baseline characteristics (Table ). Data collection and clinical definitions Baseline demographic and clinical data were collected by trained nursing staff within the first three months after PD initiation, encompassing age, sex, anthropometric measurements (height and weight), medication history (including lipid-lowering drugs, glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants use), self-reported medical conditions (including diabetes and cardiovascular disease [CVD]), and comprehensive laboratory results. All laboratory analyses—including routine blood tests, biochemical profiles, renal/liver function tests, and lipid panels—were performed at Nanfang Hospital’s central laboratory following standardized operating procedures. The first three months of peritoneal dialysis represent a critical adaptation period characterized by physiological adjustments and potential metabolic instability. To account for natural fluctuations in lipid levels during this phase and to obtain a more stable baseline measurement, all laboratory values—including HDL-C—were calculated as the mean of all available determinations obtained during the initial three months following PD commencement. PD-specific assessments were conducted per established protocols [ , ], including total weekly CrCl, weekly Kt/V, and peritoneal equilibration test (PET) results. Total weekly Kt/V was calculated by integrating urea concentrations in the 24-hour dialysate and urine, their respective volumes, and serum urea levels. Total weekly CrCl was determined by combining dialysate and urine creatinine concentrations, urine output, and residual renal function [ ]. PET was performed to classify peritoneal transport function into four types (low, low-average, high-average, and high) based on the 4-hour dialysate-to-plasma creatinine ratio (D/Pcr) [ ]. CVD was defined as physician-diagnosed heart failure, myocardial infarction, or cerebrovascular accident. Diabetes was diagnosed by clinicians based on the patient’s medical history, medication use, fasting blood glucose, and/or postprandial blood glucose levels. Body mass index (BMI) was calculated by dividing weight (kg) by square of standing height (m). The study’s principal exposure variable was baseline serum HDL-C concentration, stratified into three clinically relevant categories based on established cut points [ ]: low ( < 40 mg/dL), normal (40–60 mg/dL), and high (≥60 mg/dL). This classification enabled examination of potential non-linear associations with clinical outcomes while maintaining clinical interpretability. Study outcomes and follow-up The primary outcome was new-onset PDRP, diagnosed according to 2017 ISPD guidelines [ ] when meeting ≥2 criteria: (1) abdominal pain with/without cloudy effluent or fever; (2) effluent leukocyte count ≥100 × 10 6 cells/L ( > 50% polymorphonuclear cells); or (3) positive effluent Gram stain/culture. Pathogen distribution in participants with PDRP stratified by HDL-C concentrations was presented in Fig. . To avoid confounding by procedural factors, we excluded catheter insertion-related peritonitis (occurring ≤30 days post-insertion). Patients were routinely evaluated every 2 months (first year) and 5 months (subsequently) until December 31, 2023. Follow-up terminated at PDRP onset, death, or PD discontinuation. Patients transitioning to hemodialysis, receiving transplants, transferring centers, or lost to follow-up were censored at their last documented clinical encounter. Statistical analysis Baseline characteristics were presented as mean (standard deviation, SD) or median (interquartile range [IQR]) for continuous variables and as frequencies (percentages) for categorical variables. Differences across HDL-C categories were assessed using ANOVA for continuous variables and chi-square (χ 2 ) tests for categorical variables. We initially examined the dose-response relationship between HDL-C concentrations and PDRP risk using restricted cubic splines (RCS). Kaplan-Meier curves were generated to compare cumulative PDRP incidence among HDL-C categories. Multivariable Cox regression models were constructed to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs): Model 1 adjusted for age, sex, and BMI; Model 2 additionally adjusted diabetes history, CVD, medication use of lipid-lowering drugs, glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants, serum albumin, CRP, intact parathyroid hormone (iPTH), potassium, lipid profiles (triglycerides, total cholesterol, LDL-C), and dialysis adequacy parameters (total weekly Kt/V and CrCl). Missing data for normally distributed variables (e.g., potassium, albumin, BMI) were imputed using mean values, whereas missing data for non-normally distributed variables (e.g., CRP, iPTH, weekly CrCl, and Kt/V) were imputed using median values. Baseline characteristics of participants with complete-case were presented in Table . Subgroup analyses evaluated effect modification by age ( < 60 vs. ≥60 years), sex, BMI ( < 24 vs. ≥24 kg/m 2 ), diabetes status, CVD history, dialysis vintage ( < 36 vs. ≥36 months), Kt/V ( < 2.2 vs. ≥2.2), and CRP concentrations ( < 3.0 vs. ≥3.0 mg/L), with interaction terms testing for heterogeneity. We performed four sensitivity analyses to verify the robustness of our findings: (1) excluding patients with pre-existing CVD; (2) repeating analyses using complete-case data without imputation; (3) implementing competing risk regression (Fine-Gray subdistribution models) with death, kidney transplantation, or transition to hemodialysis as competing events; and (4) applying multiple imputation techniques for missing data. A two-tailed p < 0.05 was considered to be statistically significant. R software (version 4.1.3, http://www.R-project.org ) was used for all statistical analyses. Results Baseline characteristics of study participants The final cohort comprised 512 patients with a mean age of 43.1 years (SD 14.1), including 216 (42.2%) female participants, as detailed in Fig. . Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics are presented in Table . Compared to patients with low HDL-C concentrations, those with high HDL-C concentrations were more likely to female, had lower BMI, higher use of lipid-lowering drugs, elevated concentrations of total cholesterol and LDL-C, greater total weekly Kt/V and total weekly CrCl, as well as had longer dialysis vintage. Included subjects and subjects with complete-case had comparable baseline characteristics (Table and Table ). Associations between HDL-C concentrations and the risk of new-onset PDRP During the median follow-up of 45.0 months (IQR 22.0–67.2), we observed the following outcomes among the 512 PD patients: 156 (30.5%) developed new-onset PDRP, 107 (20.9%) died, 104 (20.3%) transitioned to hemodialysis, 150 (29.3%) underwent renal transplantation, and 21 (4.1%) were lost to follow-up (Fig. ). In the group with HDL-C > 60 mg/dL, Gram-negative bacteria accounted for a significantly higher proportion of infections (33%) compared to both the < 40 mg/dL and 40–60 mg/dL groups (20% each). Discussion Our study reveals a significant inverse association between HDL-C concentrations and the risk of new-onset PDRP. Patients with high HDL-C concentrations (≥60 mg/dL) showed a remarkable 60% reduction in PDRP incidence compared to those with low HDL-C concentrations ( < 40 mg/dL). The current evidence regarding HDL-C and PDRP risk remains inconclusive. While one recent study reported an increased PDRP risk in diabetic patients with low HDL-C concentrations [ ], its multivariate analysis failed to evaluate the independent effect of HDL-C. Another study found no significant association but only examined HDL-C as a continuous variable, overlooking potential risk differences across clinically meaningful HDL-C strata [ ]. Importantly, neither study [ , ] accounted for key confounding factors such as CRP concentrations, total weekly Kt/V, or CrCl, which could substantially affect the outcomes. Our study provides robust evidence addressing current knowledge gaps in this field. We identified a significant inverse association between HDL-C concentrations and new-onset PDRP risk, demonstrating that patients with normal or elevated HDL-C concentrations had substantially lower risk compared to those with low HDL-C concentrations. This association is strongly supported by multiple established biological mechanisms involving HDLs immunomodulatory functions. Although the cumulative incidence of PDRP among the three HDL-C subgroups is modest (log-rank p = 0.048), the finding carries substantial clinical importance, as it demonstrates a clear dose-response relationship where higher HDL-C levels (particularly ≥60 mg/dL) correspond to dramatically reduced PDRP risk—with 60 and 35% risk reductions in the high and normal groups, respectively. This suggests that HDL-C may serve as a modifiable marker for risk stratification in peritoneal dialysis patients, highlighting its potential clinical relevance in identifying individuals at elevated risk. However, further research is required to validate its utility in guiding clinical risk assessment, and well-designed intervention studies would be necessary to explore any potential therapeutic applications in this population. The protective effects of HDL-C are mediated through several distinct pathways. HDL binds pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) including LPS (Gram-negative bacteria) and LTA (Gram-positive bacteria), blocking their interaction with Toll-like receptors 4 (TLR4) that initiate inflammatory cascades [ – ]. Additionally, HDL facilitates endotoxin clearance via hepatic SR-BI receptors [ , ], while its core component apolipoprotein A-I (ApoA-I) mitigates endotoxemia-induced organ damage and monocyte activation [ ]. Emerging research further reveals HDLs dual role in infection defense: while promoting cholesterol efflux induces pro-inflammatory macrophage responses, HDL simultaneously enhances bacterial phagocytosis. Animal models with elevated HDL demonstrate superior bacterial clearance capacity [ ], indicating HDL protects against infections through both PAMP neutralization and macrophage function enhancement. Within the local peritoneal environment, ApoA-I, the major structural component of HDL-C, plays a critical protective role. It contributes to the maintenance of peritoneal membrane integrity and ultrafiltration capacity in PD patients by suppressing local inflammation, oxidative stress, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) [ ]. Conversely, reduced ApoA-I levels may compromise peritoneal host defense mechanisms, thereby elevating the risk of peritonitis. Additionally, dyslipidemia can promote peritoneal injury through multiple complementary pathways, such as intracellular lipid accumulation and lipotoxicity, interaction with the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), endothelial dysfunction, and interplay with high-glucose conditions in PD solution and its metabolites—including advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) and glucose degradation products (GDPs). Together, these processes foster a pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic peritoneal microenvironment [ ]. This elaborated mechanistic framework is further corroborated by recent evidence demonstrating the anti-infective capacity of HDL constituents in peritonitis [ ]. Notably, although our study did

Additionally, dyslipidemia can promote peritoneal injury through multiple complementary pathways, such as intracellular lipid accumulation and lipotoxicity, interaction with the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), endothelial dysfunction, and interplay with high-glucose conditions in PD solution and its metabolites—including advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) and glucose degradation products (GDPs). Together, these processes foster a pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic peritoneal microenvironment [ ]. This elaborated mechanistic framework is further corroborated by recent evidence demonstrating the anti-infective capacity of HDL constituents in peritonitis [ ]. Notably, although our study did not identify a significant modifying effect of CRP, we observed a stronger inverse association between HDL-C and PDRP risk in participants with elevated CRP (≥3.0 mg/L; HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.55–1.03) compared to those with lower CRP ( < 3.0 mg/L; HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.38–0.80). These findings further suggest a potential role of systemic inflammation on HDL-C’s protective effects, warranting further investigation into the underlying mechanisms. Several study limitations merit consideration. First, the observational nature of our study precludes definitive causal inferences regarding the HDL-C-PDRP association. Second, while we accounted for numerous potential confounders, residual confounding from unmeasured variables (e.g., nutritional status, immunosuppressive medications, or genetic factors) remains possible. Third, the generalizability of our findings may be limited by the relatively young age of our cohort (mean age 43 years). Further investigation in older and more ethnically diverse populations is warranted to confirm and extend our results. Fourth, as the study population was drawn from a single center in southern China, the findings may not be generalizable to populations with different demographics, dietary habits, peritoneal dialysis practices, or genetic backgrounds. Fifth, an important limitation of our study is the reliance on a single baseline measurement of lipid levels, including HDL-C, can fluctuate during long-term dialysis and in response to intercurrent illnesses or changes in nutritional status. These temporal variations could potentially attenuate the observed associations, meaning our results might underestimate the true strength of the relationship between persistently low HDL-C levels and PDRP risk. Future studies incorporating serial HDL-C measurements would be valuable to better characterize this dynamic relationship. Conclusions In this retrospective single-center study, we observed a significant inverse association between serum HDL-C levels and the risk of new-onset PDRP. However, our findings must be interpreted as hypothesis-generating due to the inherent limitations of the observational design, and they do not establish causality. Future large-scale, multicenter prospective studies are warranted to confirm this association and to explore its underlying mechanisms. If validated, maintaining optimal HDL-C levels may represent a potential preventive strategy against PDRP in patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis.
